content: The RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine is designed to target regions with perennial malaria transmission that experience seasonal peaks. The vaccination strategy aims to align the period of highest vaccine efficacy, which occurs shortly after administration, with the time of peak malaria transmission. The primary vaccination series consists of three doses administered at monthly intervals, followed by annual booster doses prior to the peak transmission season. Countries implementing a seasonal deployment of the RTS,S/AS01 vaccine are encouraged to document their experiences, including vaccine effectiveness, feasibility, and any adverse events following immunization. This data will contribute to future updates of the guidance. The World Health Organization (WHO) also urges international and national funders to support learning opportunities related to vaccine deployment. The RTS,S/AS01 vaccine has been evaluated for co-administration with routine childhood vaccines in several trials. Non-inferiority criteria were met for all vaccines administered alongside RTS,S/AS01 compared to their administration without it. The vaccine can be given concurrently with monovalent or combination vaccines, including those for diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (both whole-cell and acellular), hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b, oral polio, measles, rubella, yellow fever, rotavirus, and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines. However, no co-administration studies have been conducted with vaccines for meningococcus A, typhoid conjugate, cholera, Japanese encephalitis, tick-borne encephalitis, rabies, mumps, influenza, or varicella. The RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine is recommended for the prevention of Plasmodium falciparum malaria in children living in regions with moderate to high transmission, as defined by WHO. It should be administered in a four-dose schedule starting at five months of age. In areas with highly seasonal malaria or perennial transmission with seasonal peaks, a five-dose seasonal strategy may be considered. Countries adopting this strategy should document their experiences, including adverse events following immunization. The vaccine should be integrated into a comprehensive malaria control strategy. Decisions on where to introduce the vaccine should be made within the context of national malaria intervention planning, considering subnational tailoring based on variations in malaria epidemiology, health system structure, and other contextual factors. WHO defines moderate to high transmission settings as those with an annual incidence exceeding approximately 250 cases per 1,000 population or a prevalence of P. falciparum infection in children aged 2–10 years (PfPR2-10) of about 10% or more. These values are indicative and not strict thresholds. The RTS,S/AS01 vaccine is safe and well-tolerated. There is a small risk of febrile seizures within seven days of vaccination, primarily within 2–3 days. Proper planning and staff training for pharmacovigilance should precede vaccine introduction. The only contraindication is severe hypersensitivity to any vaccine component. Malnourished or HIV-positive infants may be vaccinated using the standard schedule, as the vaccine has been shown to be safe in these groups. It is also recommended for children aged 5–17 months who relocate to areas of moderate to high transmission, including during emergency situations. The vaccine is not recommended for adults or travelers, who should instead use chemoprophylaxis and vector control methods. Post-introduction monitoring of the vaccine’s effectiveness and safety is essential. Countries using the five-dose seasonal strategy should document their experiences, including adverse events. Operational research is needed to optimize the seasonal delivery of vaccine doses, including annual pre-season dosing after the primary series. Further evaluation is required to determine the best approach for combining seasonal malaria vaccination with seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC). Data collection on safety, immunogenicity, and effectiveness of annual doses beyond the fifth dose is also necessary. The additional visits required for RTS,S/AS01 vaccination provide opportunities to deliver other integrated and preventive health services, such as catching up on missed vaccinations, administering Vitamin A, deworming, and reinforcing the importance of using insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) and seeking prompt diagnosis and treatment for fever. Given the expected limited supply of the RTS,S/AS01 vaccine in the short to medium term and high demand, WHO is working with partners to develop a framework for allocating the initial limited doses. This framework will incorporate market dynamics, learning from experience, scientific evidence, implementation considerations, and social values, including fairness and equity. Clinical trials and pilot implementation studies have demonstrated the vaccine’s meaningful impact, including significant reductions in clinical malaria (51%), severe malaria (45%), and malaria-related hospitalizations (37%) after 12 months of follow-up for the first three doses. Over 46 months of follow-up, reductions in clinical malaria (39%), severe malaria (29%), severe malaria anemia (61%), and the need for blood transfusions (30%) were observed among children who received a fourth dose 18 months after the third dose. The vaccine averted 1,774 clinical malaria cases per 1,000 vaccinated children over 46 months. In areas of moderate to high transmission, the vaccine reduced uncomplicated malaria (63%), hospital admissions with severe malaria (70%), and malaria-related deaths (73%) when combined with SMC compared to SMC alone. The vaccine’s safety profile has been extensively reviewed. While rare safety signals, such as an excess of meningitis and cerebral malaria, were identified in Phase 3 trials, these were not causally linked to the vaccine. Additional safety signals, including an excess of deaths among girls compared to boys, were also not found to be causally related. These findings were not observed in Phase 2 trials or subsequent Phase 3 trials. The RTS,S/AS01 vaccine is a critical tool in reducing childhood illness and mortality due to malaria, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. Preferences and values of the target population indicate high acceptance of the vaccine, driven by its perceived health benefits. Coverage data suggests that the vaccine does not negatively impact the uptake of other childhood vaccinations, ITN use, or health-seeking behavior for febrile illness. Mathematical models predict that the vaccine is cost-effective, with a cost per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted comparable to other new vaccines and malaria interventions.
